categories.name: Mathematics
categories.description: Number, structure, shape and proof, from the invention of zero to the mathematics of unpredictability.

categories.name: Physics
categories.description: Matter, energy, motion and the laws that connect a kettle to a black hole.

categories.name: Astronomy and Space
categories.description: The contents and history of the sky, and the instruments and probes sent to read it.

categories.name: Chemistry and Materials
categories.description: Atoms, bonds and reactions, and the long road from alchemy to the periodic table.

categories.name: Life Sciences
categories.description: Living systems from molecules to reefs, and the evolutionary logic behind them.

categories.name: Medicine and the Mind
categories.description: How medical knowledge was established, and how bodies and memory actually work.

categories.name: Earth and Environment
categories.description: The planet as a working machine: crust, water, ice, air and the cycles that link them.

categories.name: Geography and Places
categories.description: Specific places on Earth, why they ended up that way, and the craft of mapping them.

categories.name: Computing and Information
categories.description: Computation, cryptography, networks and information as a measurable quantity.

categories.name: Engineering and Technology
categories.description: Machines and instruments, from bronze gearwork to satellites that keep time.

categories.name: History
categories.description: Periods, events and exchange networks that reshaped how people lived and thought.

categories.name: Philosophy and Religion
categories.description: Traditions of reasoning, belief and conduct, and the arguments that outlived them.

categories.name: Language and Literature
categories.description: Writing systems, languages and the works that survived long enough to matter.

categories.name: Visual Arts
categories.description: Images and image-making: pigment, geometry, printing and paint.

categories.name: Music and Performance
categories.description: Sound organised on purpose: tuning systems, styles, instruments and ensembles.

categories.name: Society and Everyday Life
categories.description: Money, records, trade goods and games, and the ordinary things with extraordinary histories.

articles.title: Zero
articles.angle: How a placeholder mark became a number: Babylonian gaps, Brahmagupta's rules, the route through Arabic mathematics into Europe, and why positional notation made arithmetic mechanical.

articles.title: Prime number
articles.angle: Primes as the multiplicative atoms: the sieve of Eratosthenes, Euclid's infinitude proof, how they are distributed, and why factoring being hard keeps modern secrets.

articles.title: Euclid's Elements
articles.angle: The most reprinted textbook in history: definitions, postulates and propositions, the axiomatic method it taught the West, and the parallel postulate that eventually cracked open other geometries.

articles.title: Calculus
articles.angle: Limits, derivatives and integrals built up from motion problems; the Newton-Leibniz priority dispute; and how rates of change became the default language of physics and engineering.

articles.title: Fourier transform
articles.angle: Any signal as a sum of pure waves: Fourier's heat problem, thinking in the frequency domain, the fast Fourier transform, and its use in sound, images and seismology.

articles.title: Probability theory
articles.angle: From gambling puzzles to Kolmogorov's axioms: expectation, the law of large numbers, Bayesian updating, and why physics and biology cannot do without chance.

articles.title: Chaos theory
articles.angle: Deterministic systems that stay unpredictable: Lorenz's rounded-off weather run, sensitive dependence, strange attractors, and what the butterfly effect does and does not claim.

articles.title: Möbius strip
articles.angle: A surface with one side and one edge: how to make one from a strip of paper, what happens when you cut it down the middle, and why orientability matters.

articles.title: Isaac Newton
articles.angle: The laws of motion and universal gravitation, the Principia, optics and the calculus, alongside the alchemy, the Royal Mint years and the feuds the textbook version leaves out.

articles.title: Thermodynamics
articles.angle: The four laws, the difference between heat and work, efficiency limits, and how a science born in boiler rooms and breweries ended up constraining stars and cells alike.

articles.title: Entropy
articles.angle: One word with two great meanings: Clausius's bookkeeping of waste heat, Boltzmann's counting of microstates, Shannon's measure of surprise, and the arrow of time that follows.

articles.title: Electromagnetism
articles.angle: Electricity and magnetism unified: fields and induction, Maxwell's equations, the realisation that light is an electromagnetic wave, and the technologies that followed.

articles.title: Light
articles.angle: Ray, wave and photon accounts side by side: reflection and refraction, measuring the speed of light, colour and lenses, and how images are formed.

articles.title: Special relativity
articles.angle: Two postulates and their consequences: the loss of absolute simultaneity, time dilation and length contraction, mass-energy equivalence, and the muon and satellite evidence.

articles.title: General relativity
articles.angle: Gravity as curvature: the equivalence principle, the field equations in words, and the classic tests from Mercury's precession to eclipse starlight deflection.

articles.title: Quantum mechanics
articles.angle: Quantisation, wave-particle duality, uncertainty and superposition told through the experiments that forced each idea, plus what the theory explains about chemistry and transistors.

articles.title: Sound
articles.angle: Pressure waves in matter: pitch, loudness and timbre, resonance and standing waves, the limits of hearing, and the loudest events ever measured.

articles.title: The Solar System
articles.angle: A tour of Sun, planets, moons and small bodies, how the system condensed from a disc of gas and dust, and the sheer scale of the distances involved.

articles.title: Mercury (planet)
articles.angle: The smallest and fastest planet: a cratered crust, an oversized iron core, a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance, polar ice in permanent shadow, and the precession that tested gravity.

articles.title: Mercury
articles.angle: Disambiguation page separating the innermost planet, the liquid metal element, and the Roman messenger god who gave both of them their name.

articles.title: The Copernican Revolution
articles.angle: Heliocentrism from De revolutionibus through Kepler's ellipses and Galileo's telescope to Newton's gravitation, and how slowly and unevenly the idea won.

articles.title: Galileo Galilei
articles.angle: Telescopic discoveries, inclined-plane experiments and the mathematisation of motion, then the trial and the long argument about what it meant.

articles.title: Black hole
articles.angle: From escape velocity to event horizons: how stars collapse, what tidal forces and Hawking radiation mean, why horizons carry enormous entropy, and how one was finally imaged.

articles.title: Solar eclipse
articles.angle: A coincidence of angular sizes: the saros cycle that let ancient scribes predict eclipses, what totality actually looks like, and the 1919 expedition that tested gravity.

articles.title: Voyager program
articles.angle: Two probes, a planetary alignment that recurs roughly every 176 years, the Golden Record's music and greetings, and what it means that both craft are now beyond the heliosphere.

articles.title: The periodic table
articles.angle: How the elements were ordered, Mendeleev's gaps and successful predictions, periodicity explained by electron shells, where the elements were forged, and how to read a modern table.

articles.title: Atomic theory
articles.angle: From Democritus to measurement: Dalton's ratios, Brownian motion, Rutherford's foil experiment, isotopes, and the shell picture that replaced the plum pudding.

articles.title: Chemical bond
articles.angle: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding plus hydrogen bonds: electronegativity, geometry and strength, and why they explain both water and the double helix.

articles.title: Water
articles.angle: A small polar molecule with a startling list of anomalies: hydrogen bonding, ice that floats, huge heat capacity, surface tension, and what each one does for the planet.

articles.title: Combustion
articles.angle: Oxidation and flame chemistry: Lavoisier's overthrow of phlogiston, what a flame is made of, and fire's place in engines, smelting and the carbon cycle.

articles.title: Alchemy
articles.angle: Alchemy as laboratory craft and symbolic system across Hellenistic, Islamic and European traditions, and the apparatus and techniques it handed to chemistry.

articles.title: Mercury (element)
articles.angle: The only metal liquid at room temperature: why relativistic effects keep it fluid, its long service in mirrors, hats and thermometers, and the toxicity that ended that.

articles.title: Marie Curie
articles.angle: Radioactivity named and measured, tonnes of pitchblende reduced to a decigram of radium, Nobel prizes in two sciences, and hazards nobody yet understood.

articles.title: Photosynthesis
articles.angle: How light becomes sugar: chlorophyll and the two photosystems, the Calvin cycle, the Great Oxidation Event, and C4 and CAM variants as engineering answers to heat.

articles.title: Natural selection
articles.angle: Variation, heredity and differential survival stated plainly, the evidence from fossils, islands and drug resistance, and the misreadings that refuse to die.

articles.title: Charles Darwin
articles.angle: The Beagle years, two decades of quiet evidence-gathering, the coral atoll theory he was proudest of, and the barnacles, orchids and earthworms behind the famous book.

articles.title: Deoxyribonucleic acid
articles.angle: Structure and function of DNA: the double helix and the contested road to it, base pairing and replication, the genetic code, and DNA read as stored information.

articles.title: The cell
articles.angle: Cell theory from Hooke's cork onward: membranes and organelles, the prokaryote-eukaryote divide, division, and the organelles that were once free-living bacteria.

articles.title: Coral reef
articles.angle: Animal, alga and limestone in partnership: Darwin's atoll subsidence theory confirmed by drilling, why reefs are biodiversity hotspots, and what bleaching physically is.

articles.title: Octopus
articles.angle: A nervous system distributed through eight arms, colour-changing skin in a colour-blind animal, tool use and problem solving, and a life that ends after one brood.

articles.title: Honey bee
articles.angle: A colony as a superorganism: the waggle dance that encodes distance and bearing, democratic swarm decisions, hexagonal comb geometry, and the chemistry of wax and honey.

articles.title: Germ theory of disease
articles.angle: How miasma gave way to microbes: Snow's cholera map, Semmelweis's hand-washing data, Pasteur's flasks and Koch's postulates, and the sanitation and surgery that followed.

articles.title: Vaccination
articles.angle: A history of immunisation: variolation in Asia and Africa, Jenner's cowpox observation, Pasteur's attenuated cultures, the smallpox eradication campaign, and immunological memory.

articles.title: Penicillin
articles.angle: A contaminated plate in 1928, the Oxford team who turned a mould into a drug, wartime mass production, and resistance as natural selection observed in real time.

articles.title: Human anatomy
articles.angle: The body's major systems and the history of describing them, from Galen's inherited errors to Renaissance dissection, printed atlases and modern imaging.

articles.title: Memory
articles.angle: Encoding, consolidation and retrieval; what the patient H.M. revealed about the hippocampus; why remembering rewrites; and external memory from knotted cords to files.

articles.title: Plate tectonics
articles.angle: From Wegener's ridiculed drift to seafloor magnetic stripes: plate boundaries, subduction, the supercontinent cycle, and why mountains, quakes and volcanoes sit where they do.

articles.title: Earthquake
articles.angle: Faults and stick-slip rupture, P and S waves, magnitude versus intensity, tsunami generation, and how cities learned to build for shaking.

articles.title: Krakatoa
articles.angle: The 1883 eruption: a blast heard thousands of kilometres away, pressure waves that circled the globe, deadly tsunamis, and years of lurid sunsets and global cooling.

articles.title: Ice age
articles.angle: Glacial cycles and their orbital pacing, the evidence in ice cores and moraines, and the coastlines, lakes and migration routes the last glaciation left behind.

articles.title: The water cycle
articles.angle: Evaporation, transport, precipitation and runoff; reservoirs and residence times; and why rivers, monsoons and deserts sit where they do.

articles.title: The carbon cycle
articles.angle: The fast biological loop and the slow geological one: photosynthesis and respiration, weathering, buried carbon, and what the ice-core record shows.

articles.title: Aurora
articles.angle: Solar wind, magnetosphere and excited oxygen and nitrogen: why aurorae ring the poles, what gives each colour, and the 1859 storm that set telegraph paper smouldering.

articles.title: Extinction
articles.angle: Background versus mass extinction, the big five events and their suspected causes, and how a disappearance is reconstructed from rock, isotopes and pollen.

articles.title: Mount Everest
articles.angle: How collision built it and how its height was surveyed from 240 km away and later revised, the physiology of the death zone, and the Sherpa labour behind the summit stories.

articles.title: The Nile
articles.angle: Two branches and a contested source, the annual flood and its silt, the damming that ended it, and the states the river made possible.

articles.title: The Sahara
articles.angle: Desert machinery beyond the dunes: the green Sahara of about 6,000 years ago recorded in rock art, oases and caravan routes, and dust that fertilises a rainforest.

articles.title: Venice
articles.angle: A city on millions of wooden piles: lagoon hydrology, the maritime republic, printing, glass and bookkeeping, plague quarantine islands, and subsidence and flooding today.

articles.title: Timbuktu
articles.angle: A Niger-bend city where salt met gold: Sankore's scholars and copyists, hundreds of thousands of manuscripts, and how a real place became a byword for nowhere.

articles.title: Cartography
articles.angle: Map-making as knowledge and argument: projections and the distortions they trade, the longitude problem, thematic maps, and the leap to digital geodata.

articles.title: The Amazon rainforest
articles.angle: A basin that makes its own rain: flying rivers, staggering species counts, nutrient-poor soils and the terra preta left by pre-Columbian populations.

articles.title: The Galápagos Islands
articles.angle: Volcanic islands on a hotspot: extraordinary endemism, what Darwin actually collected in five weeks, and the conservation pressure the archipelago faces now.

articles.title: Algorithm
articles.angle: From al-Khwarizmi's manuals to complexity classes: what makes a procedure an algorithm, worked examples like Euclid's and sorting, correctness, and how growth rates decide the possible.

articles.title: Alan Turing
articles.angle: Computable numbers and the machine that defines computability, the halting problem, Bletchley Park cryptanalysis, the imitation game, morphogenesis, and the prosecution that ended his career.

articles.title: Information theory
articles.angle: Shannon's bit: entropy as uncertainty, redundancy, channel capacity and noisy-channel coding, error correction, and why compression has a hard floor.

articles.title: Public-key cryptography
articles.angle: Sharing a secret in public: Diffie-Hellman and RSA explained with small numbers, signatures and certificates, and the earlier classified discovery at GCHQ.

articles.title: The Internet
articles.angle: Packet switching and layered protocols, addressing, routing and DNS, the growth from ARPANET to a global network, and the standards process that kept it one network.

articles.title: World Wide Web
articles.angle: Hypertext realised: URLs, HTTP and HTML from a CERN proposal to a public-domain release, its debts to earlier hypertext dreams, and link rot as a preservation problem.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence
articles.angle: A historical survey: symbolic AI and expert systems, two winters, the statistical turn and neural networks, game-playing milestones, and how such systems are evaluated.

articles.title: JavaScript
articles.angle: A language written in ten days: the document object model, ECMAScript standardisation, the event loop and asynchrony, fast engines, and its spread beyond the browser.

articles.title: Unicode
articles.angle: One code point per character: escaping the code-page era, UTF-8's design, historic scripts and emoji, normalisation, and the committee politics of adding a character.

articles.title: Steam engine
articles.angle: Newcomen's atmospheric pump, Watt's separate condenser and governor, high-pressure locomotives, and how portable power reorganised mines, mills and travel.

articles.title: Heat engine
articles.angle: Turning a temperature difference into work: cycles on a pressure-volume diagram, Carnot's efficiency limit, and the debt thermodynamics owes to practical engineers.

articles.title: The printing press
articles.angle: Movable type as a system of punches, matrices, alloy, oil-based ink and press; earlier East Asian printing; and the measurable effects of cheap identical copies.

articles.title: The transistor
articles.angle: Semiconductors and doping, the p-n junction, the point-contact device of 1947 and the MOSFET, integrated circuits, and decades of scaling.

articles.title: The Antikythera mechanism
articles.angle: Corroded bronze gearwork raised from a shipwreck that turns out to model the heavens, predict eclipses and track the Olympiad cycle, decoded by modern imaging.

articles.title: Marine chronometer
articles.angle: The longitude problem and the prize for solving it: Harrison's H1 to H4, the astronomers' rival lunar-distance method, and keeping time as the price of knowing where you are.

articles.title: Global Positioning System
articles.angle: Trilateration from atomic clocks in orbit, relativistic corrections of tens of microseconds a day, signal structure and error sources, and how much now depends on it.

articles.title: Astrolabe
articles.angle: A brass analogue of the sky: what its plates and rule do, and its use for telling time, finding latitude and fixing prayer hours before the sextant.

articles.title: The Silk Road
articles.angle: Not one road but a relay of exchanges: silk, horses, paper, notation, religions and pathogens moving both ways across steppe, desert and sea, and the oasis cities that lived off it.

articles.title: The Roman Empire
articles.angle: Expansion and administration, law and citizenship, roads, aqueducts and concrete, the crises of the third century, and the long transformation rather than a single fall.

articles.title: The Islamic Golden Age
articles.angle: Baghdad's translation movement, algebra and algorithms, optics, hospitals and observatories, paper-making from the east, and the transmission of it all westward.

articles.title: The Library of Alexandria
articles.angle: The Mouseion and its scholars, scroll collecting and cataloguing, Eratosthenes measuring the Earth, and why the library's end was slow attrition rather than one fire.

articles.title: Ancient Egypt
articles.angle: Three thousand years along one river: kingdoms and dynasties, hieroglyphs and scribes, monumental building, religion and burial, and Egyptian mathematics and medicine.

articles.title: The Black Death
articles.angle: Plague across Eurasia in the 1340s: spread along trade routes, mortality estimates and how they are argued, quarantine invented in port cities, and the wage and land upheaval after.

articles.title: The Renaissance
articles.angle: Recovering antiquity: banker patrons and workshop practice, perspective and print, humanist scholarship, new optics, and the argument over whether rebirth describes anything real.

articles.title: The Scientific Revolution
articles.angle: How knowledge-making changed between Copernicus and Newton: new instruments, mathematised nature, controlled experiment, learned societies, journals and print.

articles.title: The Industrial Revolution
articles.angle: Coal, steam, cotton and iron: why it began where it did, the factory as a social form, railways and cities, and the ledger of costs beside the gains.

articles.title: Revolution
articles.angle: Disambiguation page separating political revolution, the Industrial and Scientific revolutions, the Copernican turn, and the astronomical sense of one complete orbit.

articles.title: Plato
articles.angle: Dialogue as method and Socrates as its voice, the theory of forms, the Academy, and a long shadow over mathematics, theology and political thought.

articles.title: Aristotle
articles.angle: The encyclopaedic philosopher: the syllogism, causes and substance, classification and biology, the ethics of virtue, and his long afterlife in Arabic and Latin scholarship.

articles.title: Logic
articles.angle: Valid inference from Aristotle's syllogisms to Boole and Frege: propositional and predicate logic, truth tables and quantifiers, and the bridge from logic to circuits and proofs.

articles.title: Stoicism
articles.angle: Logic, physics and ethics as one system: the dichotomy of control, the Roman Stoics, and what modern popularisations quietly leave out.

articles.title: Buddhism
articles.angle: Origins in northern India, the four noble truths and dependent origination, monastic life, and the spread and diversification along trade routes into East and Southeast Asia.

articles.title: Confucius
articles.angle: Ritual, reciprocity and the cultivated person as recorded in the Analects, the making of a canon, and the examination system built on it.

articles.title: Ship of Theseus
articles.angle: Replace every plank and is it the same ship? Identity over time, Hobbes's twist with the salvaged timbers, and the version where your own cells keep replacing themselves.

articles.title: Writing systems
articles.angle: How scripts encode language: logographic, syllabic and alphabetic systems, clay tokens to cuneiform to alphabets, independent inventions, and what writing did to memory and rule.

articles.title: Cuneiform
articles.angle: Wedges pressed into clay for three millennia: accounting origins, scribal schools, the languages it served, and the receipts, omens and complaints that read like yesterday.

articles.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
articles.angle: A king, a wild companion and a refused immortality, reassembled from broken tablets after two thousand years lost, including the flood account that startled its translator.

articles.title: William Shakespeare
articles.angle: A working playwright's economics, the playhouse and the plague closures, the range of plays and sonnets, his effect on English, and how the First Folio saved half the work.

articles.title: One Thousand and One Nights
articles.angle: A frame story assembled across centuries and languages, the tales added by European translators, and Scheherazade as the original cliffhanger engine.

articles.title: Quipu
articles.angle: Andean knotted-cord records: what the knots encode for census and tribute, and the open question of whether some carry narrative as well as numbers.

articles.title: Leonardo da Vinci
articles.angle: Painter, engineer and note-taker: the surviving paintings and sfumato, the notebooks on anatomy, water and flight, the unbuilt machines, and the myth of the lone genius.

articles.title: Linear perspective
articles.angle: The geometry of depth on a flat surface: Brunelleschi's demonstration and Alberti's rules, vanishing points, and what pictures outside that tradition do instead.

articles.title: Impressionism
articles.angle: Painting light and modern life: independent exhibitions, broken brushwork and new tube pigments, hostile critics, and the pull of Japanese prints and the camera.

articles.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
articles.angle: What the print actually shows, the collaborative woodblock workshop behind it, the imported Prussian blue that made it possible, and its life as a global emblem.

articles.title: Camera obscura
articles.angle: A dark room, a small hole and an inverted image: Ibn al-Haytham's optics, its use by painters and eclipse observers, and its direct line to photography.

articles.title: Lascaux cave paintings
articles.angle: Seventeen-thousand-year-old animals in a cave found by teenagers: the pigments and scaffolding used, what the images may have been for, and why the original had to be sealed and copied.

articles.title: Ultramarine
articles.angle: Blue ground from Afghan lapis lazuli, once costlier than gold and reserved for the Virgin's robe, until a synthetic version arrived in 1826.

articles.title: Baroque music
articles.angle: 1600 to 1750 in sound: basso continuo and figured bass, ornament and affect, the rise of opera and the concerto, tuning debates, and what historically informed performance changed.

articles.title: Johann Sebastian Bach
articles.angle: A working church musician's life and output: weekly cantatas and passions, counterpoint as craft, the keyboard cycles, and the nineteenth-century revival that rescued him.

articles.title: Equal temperament
articles.angle: Why pure fifths and pure octaves cannot both close the circle: the comma that must go somewhere, meantone and well temperaments, and tuning systems outside Europe.

articles.title: Jazz
articles.angle: Roots in New Orleans, blues and ragtime; swing, bebop and after; improvisation as composition in real time; and recording's role in spreading it.

articles.title: Gamelan
articles.angle: Bronze ensembles of Java and Bali: slendro and pelog tunings, paired instruments deliberately detuned to shimmer, interlocking parts, and a place on the Voyager record.

articles.title: Bass
articles.angle: Disambiguation page separating the low register and voice type, the instrument family that plays it, and the unrelated fish spelled the same way.

articles.title: Money
articles.angle: Beyond the barter myth: credit and tally sticks, coinage and debasement, banknotes and clearing, and what actually makes a unit of account work.

articles.title: Double-entry bookkeeping
articles.angle: Debits, credits and the balancing identity; Pacioli's 1494 manual; and why the balance sheet made large enterprises governable at all.

articles.title: Salt
articles.angle: The mineral people built roads, taxes and rebellions around: preservation chemistry, Saharan slabs traded for gold, mines and pans, and why salary sounds like salt.

articles.title: Chess
articles.angle: Chaturanga through Persia to Europe, how the rules and the queen settled, notation and opening theory, the Mechanical Turk hoax, and the moment machines stopped losing.

articles.title: Game theory
articles.angle: Payoff matrices, Nash equilibrium, the prisoner's dilemma and repeated play, with tit-for-tat tournaments, auctions and animal standoffs as evidence.

did_you_know: ... that the word algorithm comes from the name of the ninth-century scholar al-Khwarizmi, whose book on al-jabr also gave us the word algebra?
... that a corroded lump of bronze raised from a Roman-era shipwreck turned out to be a geared machine that predicted eclipses and tracked the four-year Olympiad cycle?
... that the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was heard thousands of kilometres away and its pressure wave circled the globe several times?
... that the atomic clocks aboard GPS satellites must be corrected by about 38 microseconds a day, because both special and general relativity are pulling on them?
... that Hokusai's Great Wave is not a tsunami but an offshore swell, and that its striking blue came from Prussian blue pigment newly imported into Japan?
... that a honey bee's waggle dance encodes both the direction of a food source and how far away it is?
... that the Sahara was green grassland dotted with lakes as recently as about 6,000 years ago, and that rock art there shows cattle and swimmers?
... that ultramarine was ground from lapis lazuli hauled out of Afghanistan and cost Renaissance painters more than gold, which is why it was saved for the Virgin's robe?
rationale:
SPINE: Proposal 2 (interlinking). It had the healthiest link graph — cluster-first rather than list-first, with the Entropy-to-Information-theory bridge, the print-and-its-consequences chain, and the maps-and-instruments chain already load-bearing. Its category scheme and most of its titles survive, and its practice of giving every article 4-8 in-set targets is the rule I enforced throughout.

GRAFTS FROM PROPOSAL 3 (curiosity): the titles that make a visitor keep clicking — Chaos theory, Krakatoa, Aurora, Octopus, Honey bee, Coral reef, Salt, Timbuktu, Ultramarine, Lascaux cave paintings, Gamelan, Ship of Theseus, Memory, Game theory, Marine chronometer, Global Positioning System, Voyager program, Solar eclipse, Möbius strip — plus its two best structural ideas: pairing a long-range instrument chain (Antikythera - Astrolabe - Marine chronometer - GPS - Special relativity) and its Society and Everyday Life category, which gives Money, Salt and Chess a home instead of stranding them in Economics. Its "Medicine and the Mind" framing is kept so Memory can sit beside Germ theory without implying clinical advice.

GRAFTS FROM PROPOSAL 1 (breadth): the encyclopedic spine items 2 and 3 skipped or split — Marie Curie, Human anatomy, Vaccination, Aristotle, Confucius, Extinction, The Amazon rainforest, Writing systems as a single concept article, and the Revolution disambiguation page, which is the best of the three ambiguity demos because all four of its senses exist inside the set.

CUTS: (a) near-duplicate titles — Volcano (Plate tectonics plus Krakatoa cover it), Atomic theory plus Stellar nucleosynthesis reduced to Atomic theory with element origins folded into The periodic table, Turing machine folded into Alan Turing, Enigma machine folded into Alan Turing and Public-key cryptography, Non-Euclidean geometry folded into Euclid's Elements and General relativity. (b) thin or redundant places — Antarctica, Istanbul, Easter Island, Machu Picchu, Pompeii, Kyoto, Prime meridian. (c) softer humanities duplicates — Socrates (absorbed into Plato), Don Quixote, Latin, Haiku, Indo-European languages, Greek mythology, The Enlightenment, The Protestant Reformation, The Columbian Exchange. (d) three proposals' worth of framework-flavoured tech: no Unicode-plus-JavaScript-plus-Machine-learning-plus-Deep-learning sprawl; machine learning is a redirect into Artificial intelligence, not a title.

VERIFICATION (scripted, not eyeballed): 120 unique titles; 0 dangling links_to targets; 0 self-links; every links_to target and every redirect target resolves to a title in the set; every article's category is one of the 16; no redirect "from" collides with a real title and no duplicate redirect keys; all 6 featured titles exist and are feature tier; every article has between 3 and 10 outbound links and at least 2 inbound links, so hover previews, backlinks and "what links here" are never empty.

SHAPE: 16 categories, counts 5-10 (History 10; Physics and Computing 9; Mathematics, Astronomy, Chemistry, Life Sciences, Earth, Geography, Engineering 8; Philosophy and Visual Arts 7; Language, Music 6; Medicine and Society 5). Tiers: 25 feature (1400-2000 words, each wanting an infobox and 6-12 references), 88 standard, 7 short pages. Technology totals 17 titles (Computing 9 plus Engineering 8), inside the 12-18 band, and only 9 of those are modern computing, so the portfolio angle survives without the site reading as a developer blog. Colours are one muted ring at roughly 30-40% saturation and 45-50% lightness plus a slate neutral for Engineering, so every chip holds contrast on white and on near-black.

FEATURE FLAGS THE CONTENT EXERCISES: 3 disambiguation pages whose senses all exist in the set — Mercury (planet, element, Roman god via The Roman Empire), Revolution (Industrial, Scientific, Copernican, orbital), Bass (register, instrument family, the fish). 4 genuine stubs with an obvious expand-me hook and 3-5 outbound links each — Möbius strip, Astrolabe, Quipu, Ultramarine. 52 redirects covering abbreviations (DNA, JS, AI, GPS, WWW, RSA, UTF-8, Hg), article-prefix variants (Renaissance, Sahara Desert, Nile River, Silk Route), short names (Bach, Newton, Shakespeare, Da Vinci), alternate spellings and diacritics (Krakatau, Khipu, Galapagos), and playful ones that show off the "redirected from" notice (Butterfly effect, Waggle dance, Quicksilver, Longitude problem, Bletchley Park, Mona Lisa) — enough variety to stress slug collision, case handling and redirect-chain guards.

CROSS-FIELD JUMPS (what makes ten minutes of clicking work): Entropy to Information theory; Fourier transform to Equal temperament and to Earthquake; Euclid's Elements to Linear perspective; Ice age to Lascaux cave paintings; The Sahara to The Amazon rainforest; Honey bee to Information theory; Krakatoa to Gamelan; Voyager program to Johann Sebastian Bach; Earthquake to The Great Wave off Kanagawa; Ship of Theseus to Deoxyribonucleic acid; Cuneiform to Solar eclipse; Special relativity to Global Positioning System; Quipu to Double-entry bookkeeping.

SAFETY: no living-person biographies; the medical articles are framed as history of science and method (how germ theory was established, how vaccination was developed, how resistance evolves) and never as guidance; no current politics; every subject is settled and well documented, which also means each feature article can carry real citations.
